abstract: Long COVID is an infection-associated chronic condition that typically occurs within 3 months of acute COVID-19 infection in which symptoms are intermittently or continuously present for at least 3 months. Long COVID is estimated to affect between 80 and 400 million people globally, with an incidence of 5-20% in the community and up to 50% among hospitalized patients following acute SARS-CoV-2 infection. Common neuropsychiatric and mental health symptoms of long COVID include memory deficits, executive dysfunction, anxiety, depression, recurring headaches, sleep disturbances, neuropathies, problems with taste and smell, and dizziness that accompanies erratic heart rates and severe post-exertional malaise. Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms includes SARS-CoV-2 viral persistence, herpesvirus reactivation, microbiota dysbiosis, autoimmunity, clotting and endothelial abnormalities, and chronic immune activation. Owing to the variability in the clinical presentation, management must be tailored based on a patient's presenting symptoms.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2025 Nature Reviews Disease Primers article on COVID-19-associated neurological and psychological manifestations is already drawing measurable scholarly attention: it has 13 citations, places in the top 10% most-cited works for its field and year, and shows 14 documented downstream reuse events. The early record also includes one Bluesky mention, suggesting the paper is beginning to circulate beyond the citation network.

Full narrative

The article appears to be functioning as a consolidating reference for a rapidly developing area of post-COVID research. Its strongest signal is scholarly uptake: 13 OpenAlex citations, all from articles published in 2026, indicate that the paper is being used promptly in the literature. The citation landscape is centered on long-term COVID-19 research and adjacent clinical topics, which fits the paper’s focus on neuropsychiatric and psychological manifestations of Long COVID.

That uptake is also broad in disciplinary reach. The citing works span journals in proteomics, pharmacology, cardiology, microbiology, cell biology, and related biomedical areas, with repeated links to Long COVID and COVID-19 clinical research. This pattern suggests the review is being used not only within neurology and psychiatry, but also in studies of mechanisms, symptoms, and treatment-related questions across the wider COVID-19 research ecosystem.

Beyond citations, the record shows 14 instances of downstream reuse, including a Europe PMC biomedical article mention. While the reuse data are modest, they reinforce the interpretation that the paper is being incorporated into subsequent scholarly work rather than remaining a stand-alone review. The title’s appearance in repository and library records further supports discoverability and preservation, even though the article is closed access.

Public-facing attention is comparatively limited so far: the record shows one online mention on Bluesky and no broader attention footprint in the available data. Taken together, the evidence points to an article with early but clear academic traction, especially as a field-shaping summary of neurological and psychological consequences of COVID-19 and Long COVID.
